caseno:
Civil Appeal No. 31 of 1982 
From Civil Revision No. 1145 of 1980
lawyer:
Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Sr. Advocate, instructed by Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Appellants. 
Rafiqur Rahman, Sr. Advocate, Syed Altaf Hossain, Advocate, with him instructed by Serajur Rahman, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the respondents.
parties:
Abdul Latif & Another ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Abdul Mannaf & Ors ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J: The question raised in this appeal by special leave is whether a tenancy from month to month ceases on the death of the tenant or whether it is heritable. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division before whom this question was raised on a revisional application did not answer this question observing that in a proceeding under section 144, Civil Procedure Code, the only question for determination is whether the defdt is entitled to restitution in consequence of the decree for his eviction being reversed. 

 2. Facts of the case are the following Appellants are the landlords whose predecessor in interest, one Indra Kumar Homi, had filed Title Suit No. 445 of 1958 in the Court of Munsif, Moulvi Bazar for eviction of the original tenant, Sona Mia, father of the respondents alleging that the tenancy was from month to month and that the tenant defaulted in the payment of rent etc. During the pendency of the suit the plaintiff-appellants purchased the suit premises and were substituted in place of the original plaintiff. The suit was decreed ex-parte on 20th July, 1960 and in execution of the decree the appellants took delivery of possession on 18th August 1960 by evicting the tenant. Thereafter the appellants reconstructed the premises by erecting a two-storeyed building in place of the original katcha house with C.I. sheet roofs. Sona Mia, the tenant, however, challenged the exparte decree and got it set aside under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Civil Procedure Code on 15th December, 1960 with the result that the suit was restored to file for hearing. But the plaintiffs-appellants withdrew the suit on 3rd July, 1961 showing the grounds that the tenant had already been evicted and the premises had been reconstructed in such way that the subject matter of the suit namely the original katcha premises ceased to exist. The tenant (defdt) filed an application under section 144 of the Civil Procedure Code for restoration of possession of the premises to him in pursuance of the order setting aside the ex-parte decree and obtained a favourable order for restitution on 20 February, 1962. The appellants challenged the order of restitution first by a miscellaneous appeal and thereafter by a second miscellaneous appeal but became unsuccessful in both the cases; the order of restitution was finally maintained by the High Court Division by an order dated 4th July, 1979 in Second Miscellaneous Appeal No. 18 of 1964. In that order a direction was given by the High Court Division that since a two-storeyed building had been constructed in place of the original katcha structure restoration would have to be made in the two-storeyed building to the extent of the measurement of area given in the schedule of the plaint of the original suit for ejectment. 

 4. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing for the appellants has urged three grounds before us. First is that in this suit for eviction of the tenant from month to month, when the tenant was already evicted and possession of the premises taken back in pursuance of a decree, no matter the decree was subsequently set aside, the suit for eviction became infructuous and there was nothing left to be decreed. Secondly, in between the eviction of the tenant and the order for restitution under section 144 C.P.C., the landlord having vitally changed the character of the tenancy by erecting a two-storied building, the subject of original tenancy, a katcha structure, ceased to exist, and as such there was nothing left for restoration to the tenant. The third ground is that when the tenant died the tenancy which was from month to month ceased to exist as relationship between the landlord and the tenant was a personal relation between them which came to an end and that such a monthly tenancy is not heritable. 

 6. Mr. Rafiqur Rahman, learned Advocate for the respondents has argued that before the High Court Division two questions were raised by the appellants—one relating to restitution under section 144 CPC and the other relating to the application for appointment of an advocate commissioner to hold local investigation in order to ascertain the actual area of the original tenancy, but the High Court Division omitted from consideration the second question. Mr. Rahman however does not dispute the law settled in the case reported in 32 DLR (AD) 170 as referred to above. If the tenancy already ceased to exist on the tenant's death, all other questions including the question about local investigation became irrelevant. Respondents who are heirs of the deceased tenant did not inherit the tenancy and as such they are not entitled to restitution.
